2: %% Shared scientific source for the research and TMLR entry points.
3: \section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
4: 
5: At each round, a contextual-bandit policy predicts the reward of every available
6: action, adds an uncertainty bonus, and chooses from the resulting scores.  For a
7: fixed linear representation, the same feature vectors support both the
8: statistical confidence argument and the widths used for action selection.  A
9: retrained nonlinear model breaks this identification.  The query used at round
10: $s$ was $\bq_s(a_s)=\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_s}(x_s,a_s)$, fixed before
11: observing $r_s$, whereas a policy that replays the same sample at round $t$ uses
12: $\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_t}(x_s,a_s)$.  Updating $\btheta_t$ changes every
13: replayed Jacobian at once, so the current relinearized Gram no longer has the
14: predictable rank-one recursion required by the usual self-normalized argument.
15: 
16: Existing neural-bandit methods avoid or absorb this mismatch in different ways.
17: NeuralUCB and NeuralTS accumulate gradient features when observations arrive
18: \citep{zhou2020neural,zhang2021neural}; NTK methods can keep the uncertainty
19: features at initialization \citep{kassraie2022neural}; and neural-linear methods
20: place exact linear uncertainty on a learned last-layer representation
21: \citep{riquelme2018deep}.  Fixed-reference network linearizations and post-hoc
22: Laplace approximations provide related predictive-uncertainty tools
23: \citep{maddox2021fast,daxberger2021laplace}, but they do not answer the online
24: question studied here: when can confidence built from collection-time features
25: justify scores computed with current replayed curvature?
26: 
27: Validity alone does not explain why a policy should use that curvature.
28: Transporting a given confidence bound does not add statistical information:
29: on a fixed history, the construction below produces an upper width at least as
30: large as the direct reference width.  A loose certificate can preserve optimism
31: while making the bonus dominate reward predictions.  We therefore separate
32: conditional validity, certificate usefulness, and observed policy behavior.
33: In our controlled follow-up, the evaluated Hessian-transport policy has higher
34: mean regret than each comparator in every condition, despite passing the
35: recorded optimism diagnostics.
36: 
37: \paragraph{From reference confidence to an implemented score.}
38: Four objects must remain distinct.  The frozen Gram $\bVbar_t$ supports
39: sequential statistical confidence.  The exact current metric $\bV_t$ replays
40: past observations at the current parameter.  The algorithm applies an SPD
41: operator $\Calg_t$, which may approximate $\bV_t$.  Finally, a solver returns
42: the numerical upper width $\hat s_t(a)$ used in the score.  The analysis
43: connects these objects through the separate obligations in
44: \Cref{fig:transport-interfaces}.
45: 
46: \begin{figure}[t]
47:  \centering
48:  \input{figures/transport_conceptual_interfaces.tex}
49:  \caption{From reference confidence to the width actually used for selection.
50:  Each comparison is a separate certificate obligation under
51:  \Cref{asm:abstract-transport}; the schematic does not identify statistical
52:  confidence with current curvature.  All-action upper validity and
53:  selected-action sharpness concern the same realized numerical width map.
54:  The same-history reference-width floor does not order the adaptive regret
55:  of different policies.}
56:  \label{fig:transport-interfaces}
57: \end{figure}
58: 
59: A Thompson--Finsler path length controls
60: the first arrow through a two-sided exponential Loewner sandwich
61: \citep{thompson1963certain,nussbaum1994finsler}.  A second two-sided comparison
62: accounts for replacing $\bV_t$ by $\Calg_t$.  Solver certification then provides
63: an upper-valid width for every scored action and a sharpness factor only for the
64: action actually played.  The lower operator comparison is needed to return the
65: played width to the frozen sequential potential.  A one-sided upper comparison
66: alone does not satisfy the hypotheses of the closed bound studied here.
67: 
68: For squared loss, the main statistical construction is a corrected prediction
69: center.  It combines the current nonlinear prediction with a ridge correction
70: computed from collection-time features.  This identity holds for any predictable
71: parameter path inside the certified region, so the confidence proof does not
72: require the nonlinear optimizer to converge.  Historical Taylor and
73: misspecification errors enter the radius through an explicit energy, while
74: current errors enter additively.  These terms remain genuine costs: persistent
75: misspecification can make the guarantee linear or vacuous.
76: 
77: \paragraph{Guarantee and scope.}
78: The transported-UCB theorem composes reference confidence, metric transport,
79: operator distortion, solver error, and approximate score maximization, then
80: closes regret through frozen information gain
81: (\Cref{thm:transported-ucb}).  Its confidence and certificates are available
82: before the selected reward is observed.  Factor-path and prediction-Hessian
83: certificates
84: make the metric comparison operational without a small-drift premise
85: (\Cref{lem:factor-spd-path,cor:hessian-path-new}), and the corrected-center
86: specialization yields finite-dimensional and near-linear rates without an
87: optimizer certificate
88: (\Cref{cor:corrected-center-new,cor:finite-d-rate-new,%
89: cor:global-near-linear-new}).  Thompson geometry, the sandwich-to-width
90: comparison, and the UCB determinant-potential argument are established tools.
91: Our analysis organizes their obligations for current replayed curvature,
92: including the distinction between all-action upper validity and selected-action
93: sharpness of the same numerical score.  The solver interface permits
94: matrix-free CG for a fixed SPD operator when its width is certified; it does
95: not eliminate the corrected center's need for frozen-feature access or a
96: separately certified representation.
97: 
98: \paragraph{A limitation and a sharper specialization.}
99: We make explicit the elementary same-history width comparison and its equality
100: case: exact actionwise transport reproduces the reference width
101: (\Cref{prop:reference-width-floor}).  An exact endpoint Thompson-distance factor
102: is uniform and need not attain that equality for every action.  Neither
103: comparison orders the realized regret of policies that collect different data.
104: For the scaled-tanh specialization, fixed feature directions permit a direct
105: relative-weight sandwich, with a horizon-independent uniform bound and a tighter
106: category-weight construction (\Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights}).  These
107: comparisons avoid the ridge-only Hessian envelope without claiming a general
108: result for rotating neural gradients or a new confidence event.
109: 
110: \paragraph{Controlled evidence.}
111: The prespecified nonlinear-regime follow-up uses a 29-parameter scaled-tanh model
112: with dense matrices and direct Cholesky solves in float64
113: (\Cref{sec:transport-followup}); the original near-linear audit is retained
114: separately in \Cref{sec:transport-instantiation}.  Four policies are evaluated
115: in three conditions, with 50 paired seeds per condition.  All nine pointwise
116: paired intervals favor the comparators over Hessian transport.  Its bounds are
117: dominated by path inflation in the follow-up, whereas the original grid's
118: decomposition is base-dominated.  The frozen policy's own-trajectory bounds
119: also remain vacuous.  All follow-up policies, including the uncertified naive
120: control, pass the recorded optimism diagnostics; these floating-point checks
121: do not establish verified numerical certification.
122: 
123: The conditions change the reward task as well as its curvature, so they do not
124: isolate a causal effect of drift.  Post-outcome analyses measure width-dominated
125: Hessian recommendations and audit the relative-weight certificate on recorded
126: states; they do not reconstruct alternative adaptive runs.  These findings
127: concern one model and fixed teacher with shared prediction-based optimizer
128: selection.  Approximate operators, CG, and end-to-end scalability are not
129: evaluated here.
130: \iflegacyextras
131: Earlier diagnostics are retained only at their historical scope in
132: \Cref{app:legacy-evidence}.
133: \else
134: Earlier repository studies were designed for the one-sided dynamic theorem, do
135: not execute the transported score or record its certificates, and are therefore
136: not reported here as evidence for any claim in this paper
137: (\Cref{app:legacy-evidence}).
138: \fi
